research.summary: India has two direct, high-quality measurements of exactly the parameter needed, with definitions that map one-to-one onto the model's handpump-vs-motorized split. Census of India 2011 (Houselisting, instruction manual paras 4.85-4.86) defines "Hand pump" as ground water taken out manually and "Tube well/Borehole" as ground water taken out through electrical or diesel pump; NSS 76th round (2018, Report 584) likewise defines "hand pump" as manually operated and "tube well" as a bore well operated by animal, wind, electric, diesel or solar means. Measured handpump shares among borehole users: RURAL 84.1% (2011) falling to 79.7% (2018); URBAN 57.1% (2011) falling to 39.2% (2018). Later rounds (NSS MIS 2020-21, CAMS 2022-23) publish only the combined handpump+tubewell category (rural ~50% of all households in 2020-21 vs 53.8% in 2018; urban 15% vs 17.1%), showing the borehole-user pool shrinking slowly as Jal Jeevan Mission converts households to piped — JJM plausibly removes communal-handpump users disproportionately while private electric-borewell owners keep their source, so the remaining pool skews slowly more motorized. Adjusted 2024 estimates: rural 70-80% handpump (central ~75%), urban 25-38% (central ~32%). Within the motorized share, pumping is overwhelmingly grid-electric (household electrification ~97-99% post-Saubhagya); diesel is a small minority (unelectrified pockets, eastern India) and solar domestic drinking pumps are negligible as a household main source (JJM solar schemes are counted as piped). Bottom line for the model: India's huge rural borehole population is dominantly handpump-resilient (~3/4), while urban borehole users are majority electric-displaced (~2/3).

findings.source: Census of India 2011, Houselisting & Housing Census, 'Figures at a Glance' (rows O.8 Hand pump, O.9 Tubewell/Borehole); definitions from Instruction Manual for Houselisting and Housing Census paras 4.85-4.86
findings.quote: Rural households by main source of drinking water: Hand pump 73,245,349 (43.6% of all rural HHs); Tubewell/Borehole 13,898,837 (8.3%). Handpump share of borehole users = 73,245,349 / (73,245,349 + 13,898,837) = 73.25M/87.14M = 84.1%. Manual para 4.85: 'Hand pump means where the ground water is taken out manually'; para 4.86: 'Tube well denotes the ground water source from where ground water is taken out through electrical or diesel pump.'
findings.caveats: 2011 baseline, now >14 years old; use as measured anchor, not current value. Denominator correctly excludes dug wells (separate census categories: covered/uncovered well).
findings.motorized_split_notes: Census category is 'electrical or diesel'; no further split published. Grid-electric dominates domestic borewells.

findings.source: Census of India 2011, Houselisting & Housing Census, 'Figures at a Glance' (rows O.8, O.9)
findings.quote: Urban households: Hand pump 9,354,182 (11.9% of all urban HHs); Tubewell/Borehole 7,017,237 (8.9%). Handpump share = 9,354,182 / (9,354,182 + 7,017,237) = 9.35M/16.37M = 57.1%.
findings.caveats: 2011 baseline; urban handpump use has declined sharply since (see NSS 2018 row). Many urban piped households also own supplementary electric borewells, but main-source accounting excludes them by design.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Electric/diesel per census definition; urban borewells are near-universally grid-electric.

findings.source: NSS 76th round (Jul-Dec 2018), Report No. 584 'Drinking Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Housing Condition in India', Statement 2 (percentage distribution of households by principal source of drinking water); definitions section 2.22
findings.quote: Statement 2, Rural: Hand pump 42.9%, Tube well 10.9% (of all rural HHs). Handpump share of borehole users = 42.9 / (42.9 + 10.9) = 42.9/53.8 = 79.7%. Definition 2.22: 'Tube well and hand pump are bore well used for extracting ground water... If the pump of the bore well is operated by animal, wind, electric, diesel or solar means etc., it is known as tube well and if the pump is operated manually by hand... it is known as hand pump.'
findings.caveats: Principal-source question (single response, last 365 days) — no multi-response inflation. NSS 'tube well' technically includes animal/wind-powered pumps (HEMP-resilient) but these are negligible in India.
findings.motorized_split_notes: No grid/diesel/solar split published. Rural household electrification ~97-99% after Saubhagya (2019), so grid-electric dominates; diesel persists in pockets (eastern India, unelectrified hamlets); solar as a household main-source pump is negligible (JJM solar schemes deliver via pipes and count as piped).

findings.source: NSS 76th round (2018), Report No. 584, Statement 2
findings.quote: Statement 2, Urban: Hand pump 6.7%, Tube well 10.4% (of all urban HHs). Handpump share = 6.7 / (6.7 + 10.4) = 6.7/17.1 = 39.2%.
findings.caveats: Sample: 43,102 urban households — sampling error on a 6.7% cell is small (band reflects it). Note large drop vs census 2011 (57%): mostly real decline in urban handpump reliance, possibly some census-vs-NSS method difference.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized borewells essentially all grid-electric.

findings.source: Adjusted estimate: extrapolation of Census 2011 (84.1%) -> NSS 2018 (79.7%) trend, constrained by NSS MIS 78th round 2020-21 and CAMS 79th round 2022-23 combined-category trend and Jal Jeevan Mission rollout (CEDA/Ashoka analysis of MIS unit data; Data For India analysis of CAMS)
findings.quote: Measured slope: 84.1% (2011) to 79.7% (2018) = -0.63pp/yr -> ~76% by 2024. Combined handpump+tubewell as main source, rural: 53.8% (NSS 2018) -> 'nearly half' (~49-50%, MIS 2020-21) -> still 'the single largest source' in 2022-23 while piped-as-primary rose to ~40% (13% into dwelling + 17% yard/plot, CAMS per Data For India). JJM tap conversions plausibly remove communal-handpump users disproportionately (poorest households, public sources) while private electric-borewell owners retain theirs, so the remaining pool skews slowly more motorized: central ~75%, range 70-80%.
findings.caveats: MIS 2020-21 and CAMS 2022-23 publish only the COMBINED handpump+tubewell category, so the post-2018 within-pair split is extrapolated, not measured. JJM administrative coverage claims (~75% of rural HHs 'har ghar jal' by 2024) far exceed survey-measured piped-as-primary-source use (~30-40% in 2022-23); the adjustment leans on survey numbers, not JJM claims. Half a decade of drift possible in either direction if JJM converts electric-borewell villages faster/slower than handpump belts (UP/Bihar).
findings.motorized_split_notes: Within the ~20-30% motorized share: grid-electric ~85-95%, diesel ~5-10% (eastern-India pockets), solar <5% and mostly scheme-level (counted as piped). For the non-HEMP (grid-only-fails) scenario, most Indian motorized-borehole drinkers are grid-dependent.

findings.source: Adjusted estimate: extrapolation of Census 2011 (57.1%) -> NSS 2018 (39.2%) trend, constrained by MIS 2020-21 combined urban handpump+tubewell = 15% of urban HHs (vs 17.1% in 2018)
findings.quote: Measured slope 57.1% (2011) -> 39.2% (2018) = -2.6pp/yr would give ~24% by 2024; part of that gap may be census-vs-NSS methodology, and the combined urban pair is shrinking only slowly (17.1% -> 15% of urban HHs, 2018 -> 2020-21), so the decline within the pair is likely moderating. Central ~30-33%, range 25-38%.
findings.caveats: No measured within-pair split after 2018. Urban handpumps are being retired/paved over while new urban borewells are all electric, so direction of drift is clearly downward; magnitude uncertain.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized borewells near-universally grid-electric; diesel/solar negligible for urban household main drinking source.

regional_default.rationale: India-only assignment, so the default IS the 2024-adjusted India estimate: rural 70-80% (central ~75%) and urban 25-38% (central ~32%) of borehole users on human-powered handpumps. Anchored by two direct primary measurements whose category definitions exactly match the model's split — Census 2011 (Hand pump = manual; Tubewell/Borehole = electric/diesel pump): rural 84.1%, urban 57.1%; NSS 76th round 2018 (hand pump = manual; tube well = animal/wind/electric/diesel/solar): rural 79.7%, urban 39.2% — then extrapolated to 2024 using the combined-category trend from NSS MIS 2020-21 and CAMS 2022-23 plus the Jal Jeevan Mission piped-conversion dynamic. If a single point value is needed for the model: rural handpump share 0.75 (borehole_lose_fraction ~0.25 in HEMP), urban 0.32 (lose ~0.68). For the loss-of-central-infrastructure scenario, nearly all of India's motorized borehole share is grid-electric, so displacement is only modestly lower than HEMP (diesel ~5-10% of motorized, rural only).

Their ranges (rural 70-80, urban 25-38) are consistent with the measured 2011->2018 slopes and the combined-category trend; verdict for those two rows alone would be PLAUSIBLE. One minor error inside the rural-2024 quote: '~40% (13% into dwelling + 17% yard/plot)' — the components sum to 30%, not 40%; this is an internal inconsistency in the quoted reasoning text only and does not affect the bounds.

findings.source: PSLM District Level Survey 2019-20, Table 7.1 'Percentage distribution of household by source of drinking water by province & district', Pakistan Bureau of Statistics
findings.quote: Pakistan Urban row: Tap Water 36.19, Hand Pump 7.32, Motor Pump 23.80, Dug Well 0.68, Tanker 6.18, Filtration Plant 18.76, Other 7.07. Handpump share of borehole users = 7.32/(7.32+23.80) = 23.5%. Provincial urban: Punjab 6.30/(6.30+33.24)=15.9%; Sindh 9.51/(9.51+10.18)=48.3%; KP 6.20/(6.20+35.54)=14.9%; Balochistan 1.28/(1.28+11.55)=10.0%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban household 'motor pumps' (donkey pumps on in-house borings) are overwhelmingly grid-electric; diesel negligible in cities; rooftop-solar-driven pumps a small but growing share. In HEMP essentially all motorized users displaced; in grid-loss scenario most still displaced (grid-dependent).
findings.caveats: Household shares, not population shares (large households in rural areas could shift population weights slightly). Some urban households using electric suction pumps to boost municipal piped supply may self-report 'motorized pump', which would slightly overstate the motorized borehole denominator.

findings.source: PSLM District Level Survey 2019-20, Table 7.1, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics
findings.quote: Pakistan Rural row: Tap Water 13.60, Hand Pump 33.44, Motor Pump 33.92, Dug Well 5.04. Handpump share of borehole users = 33.44/(33.44+33.92) = 49.6%. Provincial rural: Punjab 31.40/(31.40+46.66)=40.2%; Sindh 68.68/(68.68+7.95)=89.6%; KP 14.46/(14.46+27.79)=34.2%; Balochistan 4.42/(4.42+23.71)=15.7%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motor pumps mostly grid-electric in Punjab/KP; rural Sindh and Balochistan have significant diesel and (post-2015, fast-growing) solar DC borehole pumps. Sindh rural is strongly handpump-dominant (89.6%), Punjab rural motor-dominant.
findings.caveats: Province mix matters a lot: a rural-Pakistan aggregate hides Sindh (~90% handpump) vs Balochistan (~16%). Survey year 2019-20 — motorized and solar shares have grown since.

findings.source: National tubewell inventory literature (Banglapedia; Wikipedia water supply in Bangladesh citing sector data; Global Environmental Change 2020 self-supply study) + MICS 2012-13/2019 (rural tubewell ~95-96% of household members, category not split by pump type)
findings.quote: 'There are at least five million Hand Tubewells (HTW) all over the country that use number 6 pumps' (Banglapedia); sector estimates of '18 million tube wells, 16 million of which are privately installed by rural families'; self-supply study: 'up to 9 million unregulated tubewells privately installed since 2006' (overwhelmingly shallow hand-pumped). MICS 2012-13: tubewell used by 96% of rural household members. Arsenic-mitigation deep tubewells (DPHE) are fitted with No.6/Tara handpumps, not motors. Arithmetic: with ~16M+ private hand tubewells vs a small (but growing) stock of rural household submersibles/motor pumps, handpump/(handpump+motorized) among rural tubewell users is >~90%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: The small rural motorized share is essentially all grid-electric submersibles/suction motors (rural grid access ~99%); solar drinking-water pumps exist in coastal schemes but usually feed piped mini-networks (excluded as piped). Diesel negligible for drinking supply.
findings.caveats: No national survey splits hand vs motorized tubewell. Rural submersible 'upgrades' are documented and growing since ~2015, hence the lower bound of 88. Pump counts are not user shares, but here handpumps dominate both counts and users. Coastal zones use non-borehole sources (pond sand filters, rainwater) — excluded correctly.

findings.source: Composite: JASBS Turag-Buriganga peri-urban Dhaka household survey (motorized vs hand tubewell); World Bank urban WSS factsheet (piped systems in only 151 of 329 pourashavas, core areas only); MICS urban tubewell ~65-70% of urban household members
findings.quote: Turag peri-urban Dhaka survey: 'motorized tubewell (69.1%), piped water (19.8%), tap water (2.1%), and deep and shallow tubewell water (2.3%)' -> handpump share among borehole users there = 2.3/(2.3+69.1) = 3%. But only 151/329 pourashavas have piped systems (core areas only) and privately installed tubewells in secondary towns 'are typically shallow equipped with hand pumps'. Weighting: peri-urban greater Dhaka/Gazipur (deep, declining water table, motorized-dominant, ~8-12M borehole users) vs secondary towns and pourashavas (~25-30M borehole users, hand-tubewell dominant with an estimated 20-40% motorized creep) gives ~(30M*0.7+10M*0.05)/40M = 54% central, bounded 35-65%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized tubewells (household submersibles and 0.5-1HP suction motors) are essentially all grid-electric; standby generators rare at household level, solar negligible in cities. So HEMP and grid-loss scenarios displace nearly the same set of urban motorized users.
findings.caveats: Highest-stakes uncertainty in this region (43M urban borehole users). No representative urban hand/motor split exists. Classification ambiguity cuts the other way too: households with own submersible + roof tank + indoor taps often self-report 'piped into dwelling' (leaving the reported tubewell category more handpump-heavy), which supports the upper half of the range. Around Dhaka the water table is too deep for No.6 suction handpumps, so its tubewell users are necessarily motorized.

findings.source: ALCS 2016-17 Table 10.7 (population by residence and drinking water source) cross-walked against Afghanistan MICS 2022-23 Table WS.1.1
findings.quote: ALCS 2016-17 Table 10.7 Rural: 'Hand pump 30.5' percent of population, with NO motorized-borehole category in the instrument (questionnaire category is 'Hand pump, used on bore hole, tube well'). MICS 2022-23 Table WS.1.1 Rural: 'Tube well/borehole 29.5' percent. The near-identity of rural handpump (30.5%, 2016-17) and rural tubewell/borehole (29.5%, 2022-23) implies the rural borehole category is essentially all hand pumps: handpump share ~ 29.5/29.5 ~ 95-100%, discounted to 85-98 for post-2016 solar/electric well conversions reported as tubewell.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural powered wells are dominantly SOLAR submersible (widespread NGO and private conversion since mid-2010s) with some diesel; grid barely reaches rural areas. Most solar conversions feed tapstand/piped mini-networks and thus fall in piped categories (outside the borehole denominator). In a grid-loss (non-HEMP) scenario nearly all of Afghanistan's motorized borehole share survives; only HEMP displaces it.
findings.caveats: Kuchi (nomadic) population uses hand pumps 24.8% — included in national but neither urban nor rural stratum. Handpumps themselves are failing from water-table decline in drought years, a displacement mechanism independent of pumping power.

findings.source: ALCS 2016-17 Table 10.7 (urban hand pump 45.1%) vs MICS 2022-23 Table WS.1.1 (urban tube well/borehole 28.7%), interpreted with Mercy Corps 'Kabul's Water Crisis' (April 2025)
findings.quote: ALCS 2016-17 urban: hand pump 45.1% of population. MICS 2022-23 urban: tube well/borehole 28.7% (Kabul province 29.5%). Mercy Corps 2025: '90% of Kabul's residents rely on water pumped from borewells'; 'Until the mid 2010s, borewells deeper than 100 meters were relatively rare... multiple respondents reported drilling up to 300 meters'; solar pumps replaced 'expensive diesel-generator-powered pumping and painfully slow hand pumping'. Kabul borehole users are now mostly powered (depths beyond human-powered lift); other cities (Kandahar tubewell 43.9%, Nangarhar 70.5%, Helmand 71.8% incl. rural) retain shallow handpump-dominant tubewells. Weighting Kabul (~half of urban) at ~15-35% handpump and other cities at ~55-85% gives 30-65%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban powered borewells are predominantly SOLAR submersible since mid-2010s, with diesel generators second and unreliable grid a minor share. Critically for the non-HEMP scenario: most of Afghanistan's motorized borehole users would NOT be displaced by grid failure alone.
findings.caveats: The drop from 45.1% (hand pump, 2016-17) to 28.7% (tubewell/borehole, 2022-23) urban reflects both handpumps drying up and households shifting to piped/yard connections from powered wells. 49% of Kabul-province boreholes were already dry in 2023 (UN) — baseline drift is severe and handpump survivability in Kabul is poor regardless of scenario.

findings.source: Nepal NPHC 2021 census (category 'tube well/hand pump', 29.8% of households nationally) + Terai handpump inventory (~1.2 million hand pumps installed; ~8 households per public tubewell)
findings.quote: Census 2021: '29.8 percent of households used water from tube well/hand pump' — the census category itself conflates tubewell with handpump because Terai tubewells are shallow suction handpumps (chapakal). Inventory: 'There are 1.2 million hand pumps that have been installed in the Terai region'. Rural Terai villages have low electric-pump penetration for drinking supply; motorized share among rural tubewell users estimated 2-10%, so handpump share 90-98%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: The small rural motorized share is grid-electric suction/submersible pumps; diesel/solar negligible for drinking boreholes. Hill/mountain rural Nepal uses gravity-piped springs (excluded), so the borehole denominator is almost entirely Terai.
findings.caveats: No survey splits hand vs electric within the category. Groundwater-level decline in the central Terai caused mass seasonal handpump failure (Birgunj 2023) — hand-pump resilience is partly hostage to water tables, not just power.

findings.source: Birgunj case studies (Sapien Knows 2023/2024) + census 2021 category structure; Nepal's 'urban' municipalities include most of the Terai towns
findings.quote: Birgunj (metropolitan city): 'more than 47,000+ houses in 2022 and over 30,000+ hand pumps' — a hand-pump-per-house ratio of ~0.64, i.e. handpumps remain the default urban Terai borehole technology. Also documented: 'suction hand pumps in combination with motors, connected to a single borehole' — hybrid setups where motorized users retain hand-pumping capability. Handpump share among urban tubewell users estimated 60-90% (Kathmandu-valley electric borewell users are a small part of the national tubewell category, which is concentrated in Terai municipalities).
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized tubewells are grid-electric (suction centrifugal boosters and submersibles). The common hand+motor hybrid on one borehole means true HEMP displacement is LOWER than the motorized main-source share — many motorized users can revert to the hand pump on the same well if the water table allows suction lift.
findings.caveats: Nepal 'urban' is administratively broad (municipalities cover ~66% of population), so the urban stratum behaves partly like peri-rural Terai. Water-table decline (Birgunj 2023 dry handpumps) is the bigger threat to the handpump share over time.

findings.source: PSLM District Level Survey 2019-20, Table 7.1 (national row), Pakistan Bureau of Statistics
findings.quote: Pakistan national row: Hand Pump 23.33, Motor Pump 30.01 (percent of households). Handpump share of borehole users = 23.33/(23.33+30.01) = 43.7%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: See urban/rural rows; motorized is predominantly grid-electric with growing rural solar in Sindh/Balochistan.
findings.caveats: Provided as a cross-check; prefer the urban/rural rows for the model parameters.

research.summary: South Asia's Indo-Gangetic and Afghan alluvial aquifers make this the world's handpump heartland, but the hand/motorized split among borehole users varies enormously with water-table depth, wealth, and grid reach. Pakistan is the only country with a direct census-quality split: PSLM 2019-20 Table 7.1 gives hand pump 7.32% vs motor pump 23.80% of urban households (handpump share of borehole users 23.5%) and 33.44% vs 33.92% rural (49.6%), with huge provincial spread — rural Sindh is 89.6% handpump while rural Balochistan is 15.7% and urban Punjab 15.9%. Bangladesh has no survey split, but ~16-18 million privately installed hand tubewells and the handpump-fitted (No.6/Tara) arsenic-mitigation deep tubewells put rural handpump share at ~88-98%; urban is the big uncertainty (43M users) because peri-urban greater Dhaka's deep water table forces motorized pumping (a Turag survey found 69.1% motorized vs 2.3% hand tubewell) while the 329 secondary towns — where piped systems reach only 151 town cores — remain hand-tubewell dominant, giving a weighted 35-65% urban handpump share. Afghanistan's rural borehole category is essentially all handpumps (ALCS 2016-17 rural hand pump 30.5% of population vs MICS 2022-23 rural tubewell/borehole 29.5% — a near-perfect crosswalk), but urban Kabul's borewells have deepened to 100-300m and are now solar/diesel-pumped, giving an urban handpump share of only ~30-65% and falling. Nepal's census category is literally 'tube well/hand pump': the Terai's ~1.2 million handpumps dominate (rural 90-98%), and even in 'urban' Terai municipalities like Birgunj (30,000+ handpumps for 47,000 houses) handpumps or hand+motor hybrids on the same borehole prevail (urban 60-90%). For the non-HEMP (grid-loss) scenario the motorized-share energy mix matters: Pakistan's and Bangladesh's motorized borehole users are overwhelmingly grid-electric (displaced), whereas Afghanistan's powered borewells are predominantly solar (largely resilient to grid loss, displaced only under HEMP). Two structural caveats: households with private submersibles feeding indoor taps often self-report as 'piped into dwelling', which biases the reported tubewell/borehole category toward handpumps in every survey here; and falling water tables (Kabul, Birgunj, greater Dhaka) are killing suction handpumps independently of any pumping-power failure.

regional_default.rationale: Anchored on the four covered countries: urban handpump shares among borehole users run from ~23% (Pakistan, direct PSLM split) through ~35-65% (Bangladesh, Afghanistan) to ~60-90% (Nepal Terai towns); rural shares run from ~50% (Pakistan, dragged down by motor-pump-dominant rural Punjab) to ~90-98% (Bangladesh, Nepal, Afghanistan). For an uncovered South Asian country/stratum, use 25-60% urban and 50-95% rural, leaning to the top of the rural range where shallow suction lift (<7-8m water table) is feasible and incomes are low, and to the bottom of both ranges where water tables are deep (major cities) or rural electrification plus middle-class incomes are high (Punjab-like plains). Within the motorized share assume grid-electric dominance except Afghanistan-like off-grid settings where solar submersibles dominate.
