Survey year 2019-20 is recent enough; a newer PSLM (2020-21) exists but the claimed +/-2-3.5pt ranges plausibly absorb drift and the suction-pump-on-piped-supply caveat the researcher already flags.

verifications.primary_source_checked: Banglapedia 'Tubewell' article (fetched directly); Fischer et al. 2020 Global Environmental Change 65 'Risky responsibilities... unregulated self-supply in Bangladesh' (via ResearchGate/REACH abstracts); MICS 2012-13 WASH thematic report Table WS.1 (washdata.org PDF, text extracted and read directly); JASBS Turag peri-urban Dhaka household survey (banglajol.info article 70760, fetched directly); DPHE 2019 waterpoint census figures via sector literature
verifications.evidence_quote: Banglapedia: hand tubewells - "there are at least five millions of these all over the country... They use number 6 pumps for abstracting water for drinking and domestic use". Fischer et al. GEC 2020: "Bangladesh now has an estimated 16 million private tubewells across the country compared to only 2 million public ones"; "between 2012 and 2017, up to forty-five unregulated tubewells were installed privately for every publicly funded rural waterpoint". MICS 2012-13 Table WS.1: tubewell/borehole 90.6% of population nationally; rural piped only 1.3% (rural tubewell ~96%); urban piped 28.7%. JASBS Turag survey (as fetched): motorized tubewells 73.8%, deep and shallow tube wells 2.6%, piped to yard 16.7%, piped to dwelling 4.5%, public tap 2.1% -> handpump/(handpump+motorized tubewell) = 2.6/76.4 = 3.4% in peri-urban Dhaka.
verifications.denominator_check: PASSED. The claimed shares are correctly over borehole users, not all households. Rural: the 88-98% is derived from tubewell STOCK composition (16M private hand tubewells + ~1.8M public handpump waterpoints vs a small motorized stock), i.e. handpump/(handpump+motorized tubewell); the MICS 'rural tubewell 96%' figure is used only as denominator context (share of all people who are borehole users), not conflated with the handpump share. Urban: the Turag arithmetic 2.3/(2.3+69.1)=3% (my fetch: 2.6/76.4=3.4%) explicitly excludes piped/tap categories from both numerator and denominator, and the 54% central estimate is computed over borehole users only (40M). I recomputed both and found no household-denominator conflation.
verifications.notes: Single verdict covers both claimed strata. RURAL (88-98, med): borderline CONFIRMED - I independently reproduced every underlying inventory number (5M No.6 hand tubewells, 16M private vs 2M public tubewells, DPHE 1.27M shallow + 0.47M deep public tubewells, MICS rural tubewell ~96% with NO pump-type split in the survey category), and to push handpump below 88% of rural borehole users would require >2M rural motorized drinking-water tubewells, which no source supports. Rated PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED only because the share itself is an inference from pump counts (counts != user shares), not a number printed in any primary table - exactly as the researcher labeled it (evidence_kind: inventory, med confidence). URBAN (35-65, med): weaker. The one hard datapoint (Turag peri-urban Dhaka ~3% handpump among borehole users) verified, though with a minor quote discrepancy: the article page I fetched gives motorized 73.8%/hand 2.6% and n=1826 households in Tongi, not the researcher's 69.1%/2.3% (possibly a different table or sub-sample in the same paper; conclusion unchanged). The 35-65 band hinges on an ASSUMED ~70% handpump share in secondary towns/pourashavas that no representative survey measures; the World Bank 151/329 pourashavas-with-piped figure is consistent with substantial non-piped urban tubewell use but does not quantify the hand/motor split. I could not refute the band, but treat it as expert judgment with wide legitimate uncertainty - if anything the peri-urban evidence and rising submersible adoption suggest the true urban value sits in the lower half (35-55) rather than above 55; the classification-ambiguity argument (submersible+roof-tank households self-reporting as piped) pushing the other way is plausible but unquantified. No newer contradicting primary source found; MICS 2019 and the 2022 census keep 'tube well' as a single unsplit category. Recommend keeping claimed bounds; no correction warranted on current evidence.

findings.source: SUSENAS/BPS 2023 (category definition); Genter et al. 2023 PLOS Water self-supply study (Bekasi & Metro); CLASP/Ipsos Indonesia Residential End-Use Survey 2020 (n=5,443 hh)
findings.quote: SUSENAS 2023: 17.07% of households drink from 'sumur bor/pompa' (one category covering hand AND electric pumps). CLASP 2020 Table 1: 'Water pump 35% penetration, 93% days used per month' — 35% of ALL Indonesian households own an electric water pump, i.e. 2x the borehole-drinking share; even the poorest expenditure bracket (<=Rp900k) is at 18% and subsidized 450VA electricity customers at 31% (Tables 21-22). Bekasi study: 48% (n=144) of urban households drink from private boreholes and 'Dug wells were often used with a bucket and rope or hand pump, which was associated with a higher workload than using a borehole with a motorized pump' — i.e. manual lifting is a dug-well trait; urban boreholes run on electric 'Sanyo' jet pumps. Handpump share among urban borehole users ~= 1 - (motorized share ~0.90-0.98) = 2-10%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Motorized share is effectively all PLN grid-electric jet pumps (100-500 W); household gensets and solar pumping negligible in cities, so HEMP and grid-loss scenarios displace the same users.
findings.caveats: SUSENAS never splits the sumur bor/pompa category by pump type; urban split inferred from a two-city research survey (Bekasi, Metro) plus national electric-pump ownership. Electric pumps are also used on dug wells and for piped-water boosting, so 35% ownership is an upper-bound style indicator, not a direct numerator.

findings.source: CLASP/Ipsos 2020 appliance survey; Pamsimas technical manuals (sumur pompa tangan is a standard rural program technology); PU SIMANTU manual on hand-pump wells
findings.quote: CLASP: national electric water-pump ownership 35%, still 18-31% in the poorest expenditure and subsidized-tariff brackets that dominate rural Indonesia; rural electrification ~99%. Pamsimas/PU manuals show 'sumur pompa tangan' (hand-pump tubewells, incl. deep-well manual pumps >15 m) remain a standard rural water technology ('Sumur pompa tangan (SPT) adalah salah satu sarana pengambil air tanah untuk air minum melalui sumur bor dangkal dengan menggunakan pompa tangan'). Arithmetic: with electric-pump ownership near or above the rural borehole-user share and hand pumps persisting mainly in poorer/off-Java pockets, handpump share of borehole users bounded at roughly 10-35%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized pumps are overwhelmingly grid-electric (PLN, ~99% village electrification); diesel gensets are a thin backup layer in eastern islands; household solar pumping negligible.
findings.caveats: No national survey splits hand vs electric within 'sumur bor/pompa'. Range is judgment anchored on appliance ownership by income bracket. Older-than-2012 hand-pump program stock is partly retired/converted.

findings.source: GSO 2019 Population and Housing Census (electrification, water); MoH Institute of Occupational Health and Environment (>17.2M gieng khoan users) as cited in Vietnamese press
findings.quote: MoH Institute of Occupational Health and Environment: 'Vietnam currently has over 17.2 million people using groundwater from boreholes (gieng khoan)' — consistent with the ~20M borehole-user stake. 2019 census: 99%+ of households have grid electricity; 52.2% use tap water. Urban gieng khoan are drilled household wells that are essentially always paired with small electric pumps (may bom dien, ~VND 300-700k commodity item); hand pumps (bom tay) survive only as niche/backup hardware. Handpump share of urban borehole users estimated 1-5%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Motorized share is nearly all grid-electric; diesel generators are backup only. HEMP ~= grid-loss for Vietnamese borehole users.
findings.caveats: Neither the 2019 census nor MICS 2020-21 splits gieng khoan by pump type; estimate rests on near-universal electrification and pump-market evidence.

findings.source: GSO 2019 Census (rural electrification ~99%); UNICEF Viet Nam handpump-program history; MICS 2020-21 SDGCW (tubewell category, no pump split)
findings.quote: Rural electrification 99%+ (2019 census: 96.3% of rural households use hygienic water; near-universal grid). The 1980s-2000s UNICEF suction-handpump tubewell stock (bom tay UNICEF) has been overwhelmingly retrofitted with cheap electric pumps in the Red River and Mekong deltas; hand pumps persist mainly in remote/ethnic-minority communes and as flood-season backups. Handpump share among rural borehole users bounded 3-15%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Grid-electric dominant; small diesel/petrol pumps exist for irrigation but drinking-water tubewells run on mains electric pumps.
findings.caveats: No direct survey split found (searched census 2019, MICS 2020-21, VHLSS durable-goods tables); bound is expert judgment on strong electrification evidence. Legacy handpump stock means the true value could sit at the top of the band in poorer provinces.

findings.source: Myanmar DHS 2015-16 Final Report (FR324) Table 2.1 (denominator); 2014 Census (electrification); Dry Zone hydrogeology literature (ICEM/IWMI)
findings.quote: DHS 2015-16 Table 2.1 (verified from the PDF): 'Tubewell/borehole 15.7 urban / 32.7 rural / 28.1 total' percent of households (population: 16.1/32.5/28.1) — the single largest rural improved source. Split evidence is indirect: 2014 census electrification ~32% of households (rural ~15%), so household electric pumps were rare; Ayeyarwady Delta and lowland tubewells are shallow suction hand pumps, while Dry Zone villages (~30% of population; IWMI/ICEM: 'most villages, towns and cities rely on groundwater') use deep communal boreholes with diesel/electric motor pumps serving many households each. User-weighting the motorized communal wells up gives a rural handpump share of roughly 45-80%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized boreholes are largely diesel-engine or, increasingly since ~2017, solar-powered (village solarization programs); grid-electric is a minority. In the grid-loss (non-HEMP) scenario much of Myanmar's motorized rural pumping survives; in HEMP it fails.
findings.caveats: No census/DHS/MLCS table splits tube wells by pump type. Survey is 2015-16 (denominator fine, but electrification has risen to ~50%+ since, pushing the true handpump share toward the low end of the band). Post-2021 conflict makes newer data scarce.

findings.source: Myanmar DHS 2015-16 FR324 Table 2.1; 2014 Census urban electrification (~78%); Yangon water studies (private electric boreholes)
findings.quote: DHS Table 2.1: tubewell/borehole = 15.7% of urban households. Urban electrification was ~78% (2014 census), and Yangon/Mandalay households and apartment blocks commonly run private electric boreholes (Yangon tap-water studies note widespread private tube wells with electric pumps); yet public handpump tubewells remain common in peri-urban wards and smaller towns. Handpump share among urban borehole users bounded 15-45%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized pumping is mostly grid-electric with heavy private generator backup (Yangon's chronic outages mean genset-backed pumping is normal), plus some diesel. Grid-loss displaces fewer urban Myanmar borehole users than the grid share suggests.
findings.caveats: No direct split; bound from electrification and city water studies. 15.7% category share is households, not borehole-user-weighted.

findings.source: NDHS 2022 (PR146) - tube well/borehole 7.7% of households; DOH Level I definitions (P.D. 856 IRR); provincial studies (Capiz jetmatic; Tuguegarao communal pump-wells)
findings.quote: NDHS 2022: 7.7% of households use a tube well/borehole for drinking (national). The Philippine 'Level I' point-source tier is defined as a protected well/developed spring without distribution, 'normally serves around 15 households', and is classically a jetmatic/pitcher hand pump ('poso'); provincial water studies (Capiz 2010, Tuguegarao) treat jetmatic hand pumps as the default communal well technology. Against that, rural electrification ~95% and better-off households motorize private deep wells with electric jet pumps and tanks. Handpump share among rural borehole users bounded 35-70%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Motorized share is mostly grid-electric jet/submersible pumps; diesel/petrol gensets are a common brownout backup in provinces; household solar pumping still small.
findings.caveats: Neither NDHS, APIS ('tubed/piped deep well' categories) nor NWRB Listahang Tubig publishes a hand-vs-motorized split; band is judgment from Level I program design plus electrification. Tube-well users are a small slice of PHL (~5.5M people), limiting the stakes of the uncertainty.

findings.source: NDHS 2022 (PR146); Quezon City safely-managed-water study (poor households using hand pumps); urban poor WASH studies
findings.quote: Urban tube-well use is a small residual (urban improved access dominated by piped and bottled/refilling stations). Quezon City study: among the poorest quintile '24.1% had access to multiple sources such as piped water and hand pumps, dug wells, and/or rainwater' — hand pumps persist in informal settlements, while formal private deep wells are electric-pumped. Handpump share among urban borehole users bounded 10-40%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized wells are grid-electric, frequently genset-backed (commercial/institutional).
findings.caveats: Multi-response evidence (Quezon City figure covers several source types) - used only as a bound, not a point value.

findings.source: MoE/UNDP 'Development of Groundwater Management Strategy in Cambodia' (2020), citing IDE 2005 tube-well survey and NIS 2008
findings.quote: Verbatim from the strategy (PDF text extracted): 'Approximately 270,000 tube-wells with hand pumps are functioning for drinking water purposes nationwide. A survey of groundwater use in Prey Veng and Svay Rieng found that 91% of almost 145,000 tube-wells for domestic use were operated by hand pump (IDE, 2005). Tube-wells are commonly used with simple suction hand pumps, which can draw water from a maximum depth of around 6m.' Arithmetic: 91% of tube-wells by COUNT are hand pump; motorized wells serve more users each and rural electrification has risen from ~10% (2005) to ~86% (2021) with some retrofit of electric/battery pumps, so the user-weighted handpump share today is bounded below the raw 91%: 60-90%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: The motorized minority is a mix of grid-electric (rapidly expanding), battery-powered, and some solar pumps; grid-loss displaces only part of it, HEMP displaces all.
findings.caveats: Pump-count inventory, not a user share; 2005 vintage (>2012 drift flag) — direction of drift is toward motorization. CDHS 2021-22 confirms tube well/borehole remains a major rural source but does not split pump type.

findings.source: MoE/UNDP Groundwater Management Strategy 2020 (urban mechanized pumping statement); CDHS 2021-22 context
findings.quote: Same strategy document: 'Groundwater is also used for urban supplies in larger towns, using mechanized pumping to access deeper aquifers with higher yields.' Most urban Cambodians are on piped supply (Phnom Penh ~90%+); residual urban tube-well users in secondary towns are a mix of suction hand pumps (peri-urban) and electric pumps on private wells. Bounded 20-60% handpump.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized = grid-electric predominantly; note larger-town groundwater UTILITIES (mechanized deep wells) count as piped users, excluded from this parameter.
findings.caveats: Thin direct evidence for the small urban tube-well stratum.

research.region: Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Viet Nam, Myanmar, Philippines, Cambodia)
research.summary: Southeast Asia splits cleanly along rural-electrification lines. Indonesia (~45M borehole users) and Viet Nam (~20M) sit at the motorized extreme: no national survey splits the borehole category by pump type (SUSENAS "sumur bor/pompa" and the Vietnamese "giếng khoan" are single categories), but Indonesia's CLASP/Ipsos 2020 end-use survey found 35% of ALL households own an electric water pump (18-31% even in the poorest/subsidized brackets) versus only 17% drinking from boreholes, and urban self-supply studies in Bekasi/Metro treat manual lifting as a dug-well trait while boreholes run electric jet pumps — so handpump shares among borehole users are low (urban IDN 2-10%, rural IDN 10-35%; VNM 1-5% urban, 3-15% rural on ~99% electrification and the near-total retrofit of the old UNICEF handpump stock). Cambodia (~4M) is the opposite pole with the region's best direct evidence: the MoE/UNDP groundwater strategy quotes IDE's survey that 91% of ~145,000 domestic tube-wells in Prey Veng/Svay Rieng were hand-pump operated, with ~270,000 handpump tube-wells nationwide — a pump-count inventory from 2005, so with users-per-point weighting and post-2005 electrification we bound rural at 60-90% handpump. Myanmar (~18M) is verified at 32.7% of rural households on tubewells/boreholes (DHS 2015-16 Table 2.1) but has no pump split anywhere; low electrification (~15% rural in 2014) implies handpump dominance in the Delta while the Dry Zone's deep communal boreholes are diesel/solar motorized, giving a wide rural band of 45-80%. The Philippines (~5.5M, only 7.7% of households) has jetmatic hand pumps as the classic Level I technology but high electrification and no national split: rural 35-70%. Critically for the non-HEMP scenario, the motorized shares in Indonesia, Viet Nam and urban Philippines are almost entirely grid-electric (HEMP ≈ grid-loss there), whereas much of Myanmar's and Cambodia's motorized pumping is diesel, battery or solar and would survive a grid-only failure. Confidence is medium for Indonesia-urban, Viet Nam-urban and Cambodia-rural, low elsewhere; the single highest-value data gap is any SUSENAS/BPS or DHS microdata recode that splits "sumur bor/pompa" by pump type, given Indonesia's 45M-person stake.

regional_default.rationale: Handpump share among borehole users in SE Asia tracks rural electrification and the age of the borehole stock. For uncovered countries, place them within the band by electrification: near-universal grid (Thailand, Malaysia, most of Laos' lowlands) -> bottom of band (urban 2-5, rural 15-25, like Indonesia/Viet Nam); partial rural grid or recent electrification (upland Laos, Timor-Leste, PNG) -> top of band (rural 50-65+, closer to Cambodia/Myanmar). Urban borehole users regionwide are mostly on electric pumps because city grids predate the borehole boom; the residual urban handpump users are concentrated in informal settlements. For the non-HEMP scenario, assume motorized = grid-electric in high-electrification countries, but predominantly diesel/solar/battery in Myanmar, Cambodia and other low-grid settings, where a grid-only failure displaces well under half of motorized borehole users.

verifications.primary_source_checked: Genter et al. 2023, 'Understanding household self-supply use and management using a mixed-methods approach in urban Indonesia', PLOS Water (journals.plos.org/water, DOI 10.1371/journal.pwat.0000070); CLASP/Ipsos Indonesia Residential End-Use Survey final report June 2020 (full PDF downloaded and Tables 1, 21, 22 read directly); BPS SUSENAS March 2023 drinking-water source shares (via GoodStats/BPS); BPS SIRUSA official variable definition of 'sumur bor/pompa'
verifications.evidence_quote: Genter et al. 2023 (verified verbatim): "Dug wells were often used with a bucket and rope or hand pump, which was associated with a higher workload than using a borehole with a motorized pump." — with Bekasi private-borehole main-source share 48% (n=144), Metro 13% (n=39), both sites urban. CLASP 2020 Table 1: Water pump penetration 35%, 93% days used/month; Table 21: 450VA(S) tariff class 31%; Table 22: <=Rp900,000 expenditure bracket 18% — all reproduce exactly. BPS SIRUSA definition: "Sumur pompa adalah sumur yang cara pengambilannya (menaikkan) airnya dengan menggunakan pompa, baik pompa tangan atau pompa tenaga listrik termasuk sumur artesis" — confirming one combined hand+electric category. SUSENAS 2023: 17.07% of households drink from sumur bor/pompa (confirmed).
verifications.denominator_check: PASS. The claimed shares are explicitly over borehole users, not all households: the researcher computes handpump share as 1 minus the motorized share of borehole users (urban: 1 - 0.90..0.98 = 2-10%), and explicitly flags that CLASP's 35% electric-pump ownership is a share of ALL households usable only as an upper-bound-style indicator (electric pumps also sit on dug wells and boost piped supply). No handpump/(all households) confusion found. Cross-check supports the direction: national electric-pump ownership (35%) is roughly 2x the borehole-drinking share (17.07%), and even the poorest bracket (18%) and subsidized 450VA class (31%) exceed or approach it, so motorized dominance among borehole users is arithmetically consistent.
verifications.notes: Verdict applies to both strata. All independently checkable numbers reproduced exactly from primary sources, and the BPS category claim (sumur bor/pompa covers hand AND electric pumps) is confirmed by the official SIRUSA definition — the researcher's central caveat that no national survey splits pump type within this category is correct (my independent searches found no BPS/SUSENAS/DHS table splitting pompa tangan vs pompa listrik). Therefore neither the urban 2-10% nor rural 10-35% can be CONFIRMED from a primary table: the urban motorized share 0.90-0.98 is an inference (Genter et al. give no quantitative pump-type breakdown of borehole users — verified), and the rural range is judgment anchored on appliance-ownership arithmetic, appropriately labeled evidence_kind=analogue, confidence=low. Nothing found refutes either range; a rural-village case study (Bantul, Yogyakarta) shows handpump wells installed at 86% of families but used by only 31%, consistent with substantial handpump presence but sub-majority rural use. Urban/rural assignment matches sources (Genter sites are explicitly urban; CLASP is national covering both, without a published urban/rural water-pump split — I checked). Caveat to carry forward: CLASP is an electrical-appliance survey, so its 'water pump' is electric by construction; it provides no direct evidence on handpump stock. One quibble: the urban record's year=2020 but its URL points to the 2023 Genter paper; the rural record's low confidence should propagate to any model use.

findings.source: Uganda Ministry of Water and Environment database, cited in RWSN 'Stop the Rot: Uganda' (2024); Uganda Water Supply Atlas
findings.quote: 'The country currently has an asset base of over 63,000 handpumps... About 67% of the population of rural Uganda rely on a handpump' (MWE database). Arithmetic: 63,000 handpumps x ~300 users/pump ~= 19M handpump users, roughly equal to the ~20M JMP tubewell/borehole users nationally; 67% of rural population on handpumps exceeds the rural borehole-main-source share, so essentially all rural borehole-category users are handpump-served. The Water Supply Atlas counts deep boreholes as handpump point sources; motorized/solar boreholes feed 'pumped piped schemes' whose users report taps/standpipes (= piped in JMP).
findings.caveats: Handpump count includes shallow wells (dug wells) as well as deep boreholes, so the x300 arithmetic overlaps the JMP protected-well category slightly; policy shift toward solarized piped schemes moves users OUT of the borehole category rather than motorizing it.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized schemes are mostly solar or diesel mini-piped systems (counted as piped); grid-electric pumping rare outside towns.

findings.source: Kampala urban weathered-basement aquifer study (Hydrogeology Journal 2022); NWSC/small-towns structure
findings.quote: Kampala informal-settlement self-supply is 'protected springs, shallow wells and deep boreholes'; 'water supply in smaller communities generally consists of point sources, which include deep boreholes and shallow wells fitted with hand-pumps.' Urban piped users (NWSC, small-town solar/grid schemes) report taps, not boreholes, so urban borehole-category reporters are mostly point-source handpump users; wealthier households' private electric boreholes are the motorized minority.
findings.caveats: No direct urban pump-type survey split found; private electric compound boreholes in Kampala/Wakiso could push the motorized share higher than bounded here.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized boreholes are predominantly grid-electric with generator backup.

findings.source: Malawi 2018 Census (WASH factsheet, NSO/UNICEF); national water-point inventory as analysed in 'An analysis of hand pump boreholes functionality in Malawi' (Phys. Chem. Earth) and mWater MIS (121,161 assets)
findings.quote: Census 2018: 73.9% of rural population use boreholes as main source (standpipes 9.2%). Inventory: Afridev 52,084 + Malda 5,258 + Elephant 1,109 ~= 58,451 handpumps; '90% of improved rural water supplies in Malawi are boreholes or shallow wells equipped with hand pumps, vast majority Afridev' (RSC EWRT 2020). Arithmetic: 58,451 handpumps x 250 users ~= 14.6M capacity vs ~12.7M JMP borehole users - handpumps alone cover the category. Solar-reticulated borehole schemes (Water For People/Water Mission) deliver via tap kiosks, so their users report standpipes (= piped), not boreholes.
findings.caveats: Solarization of boreholes is the sector trend; it converts borehole-category users into piped-category users rather than motorizing the borehole category.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized = mostly solar reticulated schemes plus a few diesel; counted as piped in JMP.

findings.source: Malawi 2018 Census WASH statistics (NSO/UNICEF factsheet)
findings.quote: Urban: standpipes 76.9% of population, boreholes 16%. Urban/peri-urban boreholes in Lilongwe/Blantyre/Mzuzu high-density areas are overwhelmingly Afridev handpump community points (same inventory stock as rural); private motorized boreholes exist among better-off households but those usually feed on-premises plumbing and get reported as piped.
findings.caveats: No direct urban pump-type split; bound reflects uncertainty about private electric boreholes reported as 'borehole'.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized boreholes mostly grid-electric (ESCOM) private/institutional.

findings.source: Kitui County Water Infrastructure Audit 2016-2018 (Oxford REACH); JICA groundwater development design reports for Kenya
findings.quote: Kitui county-wide audit (Dec 2017): 460 piped schemes vs 687 handpumps. JICA Kenya design norm: 'when the population within 2km of a borehole is less than 500, hand pumps are selected; when 500 or more, motorized pumps' (generator/commercial power/solar); a representative JICA rural project = 150 handpump + 50 motorized boreholes (75:25 by count). Arithmetic: at 250 users/handpump vs ~1,000+ users/motorized point, a 75:25 count split implies handpump USER share among direct borehole users of roughly 40-60%; ASAL counties (Turkana, Marsabit, Garissa, Baringo - 700+ boreholes in Baringo alone) rely heavily on diesel/solar motorized boreholes where users collect directly and report 'borehole'.
findings.caveats: Kenya census/DHS lump 'borehole/tube well' (2009 census even lumps spring/well/borehole at 35.4%), so no national survey pump split exists; many motorized-scheme users report taps, which would raise the handpump share among remaining borehole reporters - the bound is deliberately wide.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized: historically diesel generators, rapidly solarizing under county/donor drought programmes; grid rare in ASALs.

findings.source: Nairobi metropolitan borehole studies (KEWI assessment); WASREB; drilling-industry norms
findings.quote: Urban Kenyan boreholes (Nairobi metro, Mombasa, secondary towns) are near-universally fitted with electric submersible pumps serving compounds, estates and kiosks; handpumps in urban areas are residual peri-urban installations. No urban water-point inventory shows a material handpump stock in cities.
findings.caveats: Kiosk users fed by utility or community boreholes may self-report 'borehole' rather than 'public tap', keeping some ambiguity; bound allows up to 30% for peri-urban handpump users.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric dominant with diesel generator backup; solar rising on institutional boreholes.

findings.source: Ethiopia National WASH Inventory 2 and MIS report (Water Development Commission)
findings.quote: NWI-2: 'about 60% (93,250) of inventoried rural water supply schemes are groundwater: hand dug wells, shallow wells and boreholes' - hand-dug and shallow wells/boreholes are hand-pump (or rope-pump) fitted point sources. 'From the available 12,277 rural piped systems, 19% use diesel driven generators, 65% gravity, 3% grid and 2% solar (11% mixed)' - i.e. deep motorized boreholes feed PIPED systems whose users report public taps (JMP piped). So households reporting 'tube well/borehole' as main source are dominantly at handpump shallow boreholes/tubewells.
findings.caveats: In Afar/Somali/Oromia lowlands some motorized deep boreholes are collected from directly (troughs/tanker points) and their users would report 'borehole', pulling the share down - hence the 70% floor. NWI counts are schemes, not users.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized pumping is mostly diesel (19% of piped schemes) vs grid 3% and solar 2% - diesel may partially survive a grid-only failure but not HEMP.

findings.source: Inference from NWI-2 and utility structure (urban supply = town utilities with motorized deep boreholes feeding networks)
findings.quote: Urban Ethiopian supply is dominated by town utility networks fed by motorized deep wells (users report piped). The small urban population reporting 'tube well/borehole' as main source is a mix of peri-urban handpump points and direct collection at motorized town boreholes; no direct split found.
findings.caveats: Wide bound reflects absence of any urban pump-type table.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized boreholes are grid-electric with diesel backup.

findings.source: Mozambique DHS (IDS) 2022-23 as cited in UNICEF Mozambique National Water Profile 2024
findings.quote: '23% of the rural population depends on boreholes or protected wells WITH HAND PUMPS' (DHS 2022-23). The Mozambican survey instrument defines the borehole category as manual-pump ('poco/furo protegido com bomba manual'), so the JMP tubewell/borehole input is handpump by construction: handpump/(handpump+motorized within category) ~= 100%. Motorized boreholes feed small piped systems (PSAAs) or on-premises plumbing, reported as canalizada/fontanario (= piped).
findings.caveats: Category mixes protected dug wells with boreholes - fine for pump-type (both manual) but slightly misaligned with a boreholes-only denominator; Afridev is the national standard rural handpump.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Motorized rural systems (PSAAs) are diesel/solar small piped schemes, outside the borehole category.

findings.source: Mozambique DHS (IDS) 2022-23 via UNICEF National Water Profile
findings.quote: '...compared to just 9% in urban areas' depending on boreholes or protected wells with hand pumps. Same category logic: urban borehole-category users are hand-pump defined; Maputo's many private electric boreholes feed household plumbing or small private networks (FPAs) and are reported/classified as piped.
findings.caveats: Some urban respondents with electric yard boreholes could still tick the manual-pump category in error; floor set at 80% for that.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized boreholes (Maputo FPAs, self-supply) are grid-electric.

findings.source: Zambia National Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Programme 2019-2030 (MWDSEP)
findings.quote: NRWSSP technology menu for rural supply: 'Hand Dug Wells with hand pumps... boreholes with hand pumps to small piped networks'; planning norm 'one facility for every 250' users at $7,500 per new water point (handpump borehole unit cost); national O&M framework is the 'National Guidelines for Sustainable Operation and Maintenance of Hand Pumps in Rural Areas'. Rural point-source boreholes are handpump by standard; small piped (solar) networks are counted as piped. India Mark II is the historic standard (ZAMSIF, CPRWSSP 3,400+ boreholes).
findings.caveats: No user-weighted split published; recent solarization converts borehole users to piped-category users.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized = solar mini-grids mostly (donor-driven), some diesel; grid rare.

findings.source: Lusaka peri-urban supply literature (water trusts/kiosks; private boreholes); DHS 2018 category structure
findings.quote: Lusaka's unplanned settlements are served by water-trust kiosks fed by motorized boreholes (users report public tap) plus communal handpump boreholes; middle-class compounds use private electric boreholes (often reported as piped-on-premises or borehole). Urban 'borehole' reporters are therefore a genuine hand/electric mix with no published split.
findings.caveats: Bound is judgment; Lusaka's shallow aquifer makes private electric boreholes unusually common for the region.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric (ZESCO) dominant.

findings.source: RWSN Bush Pump technology profile; national handpump stock estimates
findings.quote: 'There are currently about 40,000 Bush pumps installed in the rural areas of Zimbabwe' (RWSN 2022; older sources say 50,000+). Arithmetic: 40,000 x 250 users ~= 10M capacity vs ~4.4M JMP borehole users - the rural borehole category is saturated by Bush-pump handpoints. Rural motorized boreholes (Presidential solarized village schemes) feed taps and are classified piped.
findings.caveats: High non-functionality (over half out of action in some estimates) means users cluster on working pumps but stay within the handpump category; solarization programme could shift shares over the late 2020s.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized = solar village schemes (new, counted piped); diesel rare.

findings.source: Harare water-crisis reporting and BGS/NERC Harare groundwater study; UNICEF urban solarized-scheme reports
findings.quote: With municipal supply collapsed (Harare produces ~500 ML/d vs 800 ML/d demand), 'working-class residents are mostly dependent on city or donor drilled boreholes where hand pumps are used to draw the water'; queues form at communal Bush-pump boreholes from 4am. Low-density suburbs use private electric boreholes. Urban Zimbabwe is thus regionally unusual: a large hand-pumped share WITHIN cities.
findings.caveats: Split between communal handpump users and private-electric users among urban 'borehole' reporters is not enumerated; UNICEF is also solarizing some urban communal boreholes into piped schemes.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: private grid-electric (with severe load-shedding exposure) plus growing solar communal schemes.

findings.source: Tanzania Water Point Mapping System (Ministry of Water, mapped 2011-13; ~60-75k rural water points)
findings.quote: In the national water-point dataset the most common extraction class is gravity (piped schemes), followed by handpumps (nira/tanira, SWN80, India Mk II, Afridev); submersible and motorpump extraction points overwhelmingly feed communal-standpipe waterpoint types (users report taps = piped). Households reporting 'tube well/borehole' as main source are thus dominantly at handpump points.
findings.caveats: Mapping is 2011-13 - older than the ~2012 drift threshold; since then RUWASA has heavily solarized rural schemes, which moves users into the piped category (raising, not lowering, the handpump share among remaining borehole reporters). Some direct collection at motorized boreholes occurs in central/dry regions.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized: diesel historically, strong shift to solar under RUWASA; grid minor.

findings.source: Dar es Salaam groundwater studies (Sci. Total Environ. 2019; IWA WST 2021; The Citizen reporting)
findings.quote: 'More than 50% of Dar es Salaam residents rely on groundwater'; '>7,500 active boreholes/wells in the city'; '>40% of the city has no access to the DAWASA pipeline network'; sources are 'boreholes with electric or hand pumps', with self-supply and private networked providers pumping electrically for hours daily. Dar dominates national urban borehole users, and its self-supply stock is mostly electric submersibles; hand-pumped boreholes persist in peri-urban and secondary towns.
findings.caveats: No formal enumeration of electric vs hand pumps among urban borehole-main-source households; shallow hand-dug wells (excluded category) blur reporting.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric (TANESCO) dominant with generator backup during outages.

findings.source: Angola IIMS (DHS) 2015-16 questionnaire category structure; Programa Agua para Todos technology mix
findings.quote: IIMS water-source categories include 'Poco/cacimba: Furo com bomba' (borehole with pump) - pump type NOT specified, unlike Mozambique. The Agua para Todos programme installed both handpump boreholes and small motorized (diesel/solar) systems with chafarizes; motorized-system users at chafarizes report public taps, but direct-collection motorized boreholes exist. Regional analogue (Afridev-standard neighbours) suggests a handpump majority among rural direct borehole users, bounded widely for the category ambiguity.
findings.caveats: Weakest data in the region; 'furo com bomba' is pump-ambiguous and post-war reconstruction favoured motorized systems more than in East African peers.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized: diesel and solar small systems; grid negligible rurally.

findings.source: IIMS 2015-16 urban source structure (tanker trucks 18%+ in sampled strata, chafarizes, neighbour taps); Luanda supply literature
findings.quote: Urban Angola (Luanda especially) relies on utility taps, neighbour resale, chafarizes and tanker trucks ('camiao cisterna'); urban 'furo com bomba' reporters are few and skew toward private/commercial electric boreholes that also feed the tanker market. Handpumps are a peri-urban minority.
findings.caveats: Judgment bound; no urban pump-type enumeration found.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric and diesel (tanker-supplying commercial boreholes).

research.region: East and Southern Africa (UGA, MWI, KEN, ETH, MOZ, ZMB, ZWE, TZA, AGO)
research.summary: Across East/Southern Africa the JMP "tubewell/borehole" category is dominated by community point-source boreholes fitted with public-domain handpumps (India Mk II/III, Afridev, Zimbabwe Bush pump, Tanzanian nira/tanira), and the classification argument in the task brief holds up in the data: motorized (diesel/solar/grid) boreholes overwhelmingly feed piped schemes or standpipes, so their users are recorded as PIPED, leaving the borehole category handpump-skewed. Uganda (MWE: >63,000 handpumps; 67% of the rural population relies on a handpump — roughly the entire ~20M borehole-user base) and Malawi (58,000+ Afridev-class handpumps; 90% of improved rural supplies are hand-pumped; rural borehole main-source share 73.9% in the 2018 census) support rural handpump shares of ~90-99%. Mozambique is the cleanest case: its survey category is literally "borehole/protected well with hand pump" (DHS 2022-23: 23% rural, 9% urban), making the handpump share ~100% by construction. Zimbabwe (~40,000 Bush pumps) and Zambia (handpump-borehole standard, 1 point per 250 users) sit at 85-98% rural; Ethiopia (NWI: 93,250 groundwater point schemes, while its 12,277 rural piped systems run 65% gravity/19% diesel/3% grid/2% solar) and Tanzania land at 70-92% rural. Kenya is the regional outlier: deep ASAL aquifers make diesel/solar motorized community boreholes with direct collection common (JICA design norm: handpump only below 500 users), so rural Kenya is bounded 35-65%. Urban borehole users skew motorized everywhere (private grid-electric compound boreholes in Nairobi, Dar es Salaam, Lusaka, Luanda: ~5-45% handpump), with two exceptions: Malawi's peri-urban Afridev points (60-90%) and crisis-hit urban Zimbabwe, where working-class residents queue at hand-pumped communal boreholes (40-75%). A caveat cutting in the model's favour: ongoing solarization converts borehole-category users into piped-category users, so it erodes the borehole denominator rather than motorizing it; the main residual uncertainties are direct-collection motorized boreholes in ASALs and electric self-supply misreported as "borehole" in cities.

regional_default.rationale: Rural: community handpump boreholes are the standard point-source technology across the region (Uganda/Malawi/Zimbabwe/Zambia/Mozambique all 85-99%), while motorized boreholes feed piped schemes classified outside the borehole category; the default's 75% floor accommodates Kenya/Ethiopia-style dry-land direct collection at diesel/solar boreholes. Urban: borehole-main-source users in large cities are mostly private/compound electric-submersible users plus kiosk-adjacent ambiguity, partially offset by peri-urban communal handpumps and (in Zimbabwe) crisis-driven urban handpump dependence. Weighted by borehole-user population (UGA 20M and MWI 12.7M, both ~95% handpump rural, dominate the regional total), the regional rural mean sits near the top of the default band. Within the motorized share, rural pumping is mostly diesel/solar (partially resilient in the non-HEMP scenario), urban mostly grid-electric (lost in both scenarios).

verifications.primary_source_checked: Uganda DHS 2016 Final Report (FR333), Table 2.1 Household drinking water (de jure population, urban/rural), extracted directly from the PDF; RWSN 'Stop the Rot: Uganda' blog (quote verified verbatim); Uganda MWE Sector Performance Report 2016 water-point counts (41,112 deep boreholes, 21,590 shallow wells, 29,097 protected springs, 20,306 public stand posts, 20,236 RWH tanks); Hydrogeology Journal 2022 Kampala paper (partially verified); MWE solar-powered mini-piped water scheme documentation.
verifications.evidence_quote: DHS 2016 Table 2.1 (population): Tube well/borehole = 47.1% rural, 23.0% urban; Public tap/standpipe = 5.3% rural. RWSN blog (verbatim): 'the country currently has an asset base of over 63,000 handpumps'; 'About 67% of the population of rural Uganda rely on a handpump'. SPR 2016 counts: 41,112 deep boreholes + 21,590 shallow wells = 62,702 (= the '63,000 handpumps'). MWE solar schemes: 'a high-yielding borehole as the water source, a robust solar power system to drive the pump... a network of pipes distributing water to multiple public standpipes'.
verifications.denominator_check: The claimed 88-99% (rural) is genuinely framed as a share of BOREHOLE USERS, not all households - but it is NOT read from any survey table; no Uganda survey (DHS/UNHS/census) splits tubewell/borehole by pump type. It is a bounding argument. Recomputed: rural borehole-main-source population = 47.1% of ~34M rural = ~16M (DHS 2016); the only point-source fleet available to serve them is ~41k hand-pumped deep boreholes (~400 users/pump, consistent with known overloading); motorized boreholes exist almost exclusively as production wells for solar/pumped piped schemes whose users report public taps (5.3% rural) and thus fall outside the borehole denominator. Denominator logic holds, though one leg of the researcher's arithmetic is flawed (see notes).
verifications.notes: Verdict PLAUSIBLE, not CONFIRMED: bounds are judgment-based, not reproducible from a primary table. Three defects found, none fatal: (1) The RWSN '67% of the rural population rely on a handpump' is almost certainly a conflation - MWE's rural technology mix is deep boreholes 44% + shallow wells 23% = 67% OF IMPROVED RURAL SUPPLY, and rural safe-water coverage was itself 67% in 2016; true handpump reliance is ~45-50% of total rural population. The researcher's argument '67% exceeds the rural borehole share (DHS 47.1%)' therefore does not hold as stated, but the conclusion survives via the category-structure route (motorized boreholes feed piped schemes; their users report taps). (2) The 63,000-handpump count is confirmed to include 21,590 shallow wells (JMP protected-dug-well, excluded from this model's borehole bucket), so the x300 arithmetic double-counts; borehole-only handpumps ~41k, implying ~400 users per functional pump rather than 300 - still consistent with all rural borehole reporters being handpump-served. (3) The urban citation is imprecise: the 'smaller communities... point sources... fitted with hand-pumps' sentence could not be located in the Hydrogeology Journal 2022 paper's accessible text (only the 'protected springs, shallow wells and deep boreholes' self-supply clause was verified); it likely comes from BGS/UPGro material. Urban 50-85 remains unrefuted: DHS urban tubewell/borehole is 23% of urban population, dominated by small-town point sources; private electric boreholes piped into dwellings would mostly be reported as 'piped into dwelling/yard' anyway, which biases the urban borehole category further toward handpumps - if anything the urban low bound of 50 is conservative. Rural 88-99 and urban 50-85 both stand; no corrected bounds proposed. Rural/urban strata assignments match DHS strata. Survey year 2016 (DHS) is the latest pump-type-relevant primary; 2024 MWE inventory is current.

findings.source: WASH-NORM 2021 (FMWR/NBS/UNICEF), Tables WF.B1 and WF.B2, national water-point census (2,313,566 points)
findings.quote: Table WF.B1, Urban sector (917,937 water points): hand pump borehole 6.3% + force-lift hand pump 0.3% = 6.6%; motorized borehole 37.2% + reticulated motorized 0.9% = 38.1%. Handpump share of borehole POINTS = 6.6/(6.6+38.1) = 14.8%. Functionality table: urban handpump boreholes only 33.5% functional vs motorized 68.5% -> functioning-point handpump share = (6.6*0.335)/(6.6*0.335+38.1*0.685) = 7.8%. Public handpumps serve more users per point than private in-compound motorized boreholes (75% of all points are self-supply), which pushes the USER share back up; bounds set 8-25% with central ~15%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Table WF.B2, urban motorized boreholes: public grid power 70.3%, generator 23.1%, solar 6.6%, windmill 0%. Note urban private boreholes are typically grid-wired with storage tanks and very commonly generator-backed (grid intermittency), so the non-HEMP (grid-loss) scenario displaces well under 70% of urban motorized users; HEMP displaces all.
findings.caveats: Point counts, not user counts; HH.H1 household table lumps tube well/borehole (urban 35.1% of members). Largest urban borehole population on earth (~52M) so this range is the single most consequential parameter in the region.

findings.source: WASH-NORM 2021 (FMWR/NBS/UNICEF), Tables WF.B1, WF.B2 and functionality-by-type table
findings.quote: Table WF.B1, Rural sector (1,395,629 points): hand pump BH 15.9% + force-lift 0.9% = 16.8%; motorized BH 25.8% + reticulated 0.2% = 26.0%. Handpump share of borehole POINTS = 16.8/42.8 = 39.3%. Rural functionality nearly equal (handpump 62.9% vs motorized 60.8%), so functioning-point share ~40%. Communal handpumps serve ~150-250 people each while much of the rural motorized stock is private self-supply serving 1 to a few households, so the USER share is plausibly at or slightly above the point share. Report text: 'facilities located in rural areas (16%) are nearly three times more likely to be hand pump boreholes than water facilities found in urban areas (6%)'. Handpumps concentrate in the North (NE 27.2%, NW 24.3% of points) where rural borehole dependence is highest.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Table WF.B2, rural motorized boreholes: public grid 48.2%, generator 36.5%, solar 14.4%, windmill 0.9%. So in the grid-loss (non-HEMP) scenario roughly half of rural motorized borehole users could retain supply via diesel/solar.
findings.caveats: MICS 2021 (39.9% of households on tube well/borehole) cannot verify the pump split; bounds reflect users-per-point uncertainty.

findings.source: INO 2015 national inventory, cited in Programme National AEP 2016-2030 (Ministere de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement), Tableau 6 and section 2
findings.quote: Tableau 6 (INO 2015): 48,808 forages total, of which 48,340 'forage equipe de pompe' (PMH), 456 recent unequipped, 12 artesian -> 99% of boreholes are handpump-fitted. '6 337 678 personnes sont desservies en eau potable a travers 42 911 forages equipes de pompe a motricite humaine (PMH, soit en moyenne 148 personnes par PMH)'. The motorized groundwater stock is 937 AEPS/PEA piped systems whose users fetch at standpipes/taps and therefore report as JMP 'public tap', NOT 'tubewell/borehole'. Hence handpump share among rural borehole-category users ~= 48,340/48,808 = 99%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: AEPS/PEA (motorized, increasingly solarized) sit outside the borehole user category; their failure affects tap users, not this parameter.
findings.caveats: 2015 inventory; MEA 2018 counted 52,596 handpumps (Foster et al. 2019), confirming continued PMH dominance. Burkina is in the SSA top-5 for handpump reliance (42-61% of total population, RWSN Stop the Rot 2022).

findings.source: Inference from INO 2015 structure + ONEA urban monopoly (PN-AEP 2016-2030)
findings.quote: Urban supply is ONEA's mandate (56 centres, 83.4M m3 abstracted 2015); urban households reporting 'forage' as main source are overwhelmingly peri-urban users of communal PMH at the un-networked fringe of Ouagadougou/Bobo-Dioulasso. Private motorized boreholes exist among wealthy households but are a small minority of borehole-category users. No urban PMH-vs-motorized user table exists; bounds 60-90%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban private motorized boreholes mostly grid-electric.
findings.caveats: Urban borehole-category population in BFA is small relative to its 9.2M national borehole users, most of whom are rural.

findings.source: Universite Populaire 2017 household survey of N'Djamena 7th and 8th arrondissements, cited in 'Hydraulic bricolages: coexisting water supply and access regimes in N'Djamena, Chad' (EchoGeo, 2021)
findings.quote: '44% of the respondents used private hand pumps and another 35% used shared hand pumps' = 79% of households on handpump boreholes in the surveyed peripheral districts; the STE piped network (19 boreholes, 40-45,000 m3/day) can serve 'barely one third of N'Djamenois'. Private motorized boreholes are described as the costly minority option vs cheap manually drilled handpump boreholes. Among borehole users: 79/(79 + small motorized share) -> ~75-95% handpump.
findings.motorized_split_notes: N'Djamena's utility (STE) is itself borehole-fed but counts as piped; private motorized boreholes are grid/generator. Chad's grid is tiny, so even motorized private boreholes lean generator.
findings.caveats: Survey covers peripheral arrondissements, which is where borehole users concentrate; central districts are more piped. Chad's ~6.9M borehole users are unusually handpump-heavy for an urban+rural mix because manual drilling + handpumps is the dominant self-supply technology even in the capital.

findings.source: Schema Directeur de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement du Tchad 2003-2020, volume Hydraulique Villageoise (HCNE/MEE/ONU-DAES/PNUD 2003); AfDB PAEPA-SU-MR program docs
findings.quote: SDEA inventory 2000: 3,267 pompes a motricite humaine on modern water points (India 1,692, Vergnet 774, UPM 534 = 92% of the park); village hydraulics standard is the PMH-equipped forage. Subsequent rural programs (PNEAR, PAEPA) built thousands more PMH; motorized rural investment is 'mini systemes d'adduction d'eau potable alimentes en energie solaire et/ou thermique' (e.g. 54 mini-AEP, AfDB 2023) whose users fetch at standpipes and exit the JMP borehole category. Rural borehole-category users are therefore ~all handpump.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized = solar/thermal mini-AEP standpipe schemes (outside borehole category); pastoral stations pompage diesel serve livestock.
findings.caveats: Base inventory is old (2000) - flagged for drift - but all post-2000 rural construction remained PMH or standpipe mini-AEP, so the borehole-category split is insensitive to the drift.

findings.source: RWSN 'Stop the Rot' Report I (Danert 2022) reliance estimates; IOM 2009 water-point inventories (4,951 handpumps in 5/10 states) via Foster et al. 2019, Table 1
findings.quote: 'Handpump reliance is highest in Malawi, South Sudan, Zimbabwe, Guinea and Burkina Faso, ranging from 42% to 61%' of the total population (Stop the Rot I). South Sudan's borehole users are ~6.5M of ~11M people (~59% of population, task stakes) - i.e. the handpump-reliant population and the borehole-user population are essentially the same people -> handpump share of borehole users ~55/59 to 61/59, i.e. >=90%. Rural supply is the India Mark II borehole standard (IRC/technology-applicability assessments); motorized 'water yards' with solar/diesel submersibles are a small, town-focused minority.
findings.motorized_split_notes: The few motorized points are water yards - increasingly solar (IOM upgrades boreholes with solar submersibles) - so a HEMP scenario displaces even these, but grid-loss displaces almost nobody (there is effectively no grid pumping).
findings.caveats: No national household survey splits pump type; convergence of reliance estimate + inventory + program documentation is strong.

findings.source: World Bank Water Security in South Sudan / PID P505316 (2024); Juba groundwater study (Sci. Total Environ. 2015, 95 boreholes)
findings.quote: 'Less than 15 percent of Juba residents can access municipal water'; 'boreholes and water tankers are still predominant in urban areas'. Juba's ~250-300 tanker trucks distribute Nile water (surface category); the borehole stock sampled in the city (95 boreholes) is community handpump wells. Motorized urban water yards exist in some towns (Wau, Malakal) but are a small share of borehole users -> 70-95% handpump.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized points are diesel/solar water yards; grid pumping negligible.
findings.caveats: Urban tanker users are NOT borehole users; do not displace them in this parameter.

findings.source: MEH/SNAPE national inventory 2012 (12,815 handpumps) via Foster et al. 2019 Table 1; RWSN Stop the Rot 2022 reliance estimate
findings.quote: Foster et al. 2019, Table 1: Guinea 2012, National scope, 12,815 handpumps (MEH, 2012). Guinea is in the SSA top-5 for handpump reliance at 42-61% of total population (Stop the Rot I, 2022) - with ~5.2M borehole users out of ~13-14M people (~38-40%), the handpump-reliant population fully covers the borehole-user population. Rural motorized investment is standpipe adductions (e.g. 70+ AEP systems 1995-2010; IsDB projects still building 455-500 PMH forages per lot in 2022-2026), keeping the rural borehole category essentially all-PMH.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized systems are standpipe AEPs (outside category), increasingly solar.
findings.caveats: 2012 inventory, but 2022-2026 IsDB procurement shows PMH is still the rural standard.

findings.source: Inference: SEG piped supply in Conakry is weak/intermittent; non-piped urban groundwater is mostly dug wells; borehole users split between public PMH (secondary towns) and private motorized (Conakry wealthy)
findings.quote: No urban pump-type table found. Secondary towns are served by SNAPE PMH programs (counted as urban borehole users); Conakry's private borehole market (electric submersibles) is real but smaller than Nigeria/Cameroon coastal analogues given weaker grid and dug-well dominance. Bounds 40-80%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric where grid exists, otherwise generator.
findings.caveats: Wide bounds; urban borehole users are a minority of Guinea's 5.2M.

findings.source: DNH & SNV 2015-16 water point mapping (Akvo): 19,951 handpumps in 5 of 8 regions, via Foster et al. 2019 Table 1; PEM Mali database (pemmali.org)
findings.quote: Foster et al. 2019 Table 1: Mali 2015-16, 5 of 8 regions, 19,951 handpumps (DNH & SNV, 2016). Mali's rural PEM standard is the PMH-equipped forage; motorized groundwater is organized as SHVA/AES (systemes hydrauliques villageois ameliores / adductions d'eau sommaires, mostly solar) delivering at bornes fontaines -> those users report 'public tap' in DHS/MICS, not 'forage'. Residual rural borehole-category users are ~all PMH: 85-100%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: SHVA/AES largely solar-pumped (outside borehole category); relevant to tap users under HEMP, not to this parameter.
findings.caveats: 5/8 regions coverage (insecure north unmapped - but the north is even more handpump/open-well dependent).

findings.source: Inference: SOMAGEP piped Bamako + peri-urban PMH; growing private motorized borehole market among wealthier Bamako households
findings.quote: No urban pump-type user table found. Bamako's un-networked fringe uses communal PMH and wells; private electric boreholes are expanding with the (weak) grid. Sahelian-capital analogue (between Ouagadougou and N'Djamena patterns) -> 40-80%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: grid-electric with generator backup common given load-shedding.
findings.caveats: Urban borehole users a modest slice of Mali's 4.7M.

findings.source: PNDP commune development plans 2011-15: 6,899 handpumps in 189 of 316 communes (Foster et al. 2019 Table 1); RWSN 2024 'Functionality of water supply handpumps in Cameroon: review of data from 310 councils'
findings.quote: Foster et al. 2019 Table 1: Cameroon 2011-15, 189 of 316 communes, 6,899 handpumps (PNDP) -> scaling by commune coverage implies roughly 11-12k nationally. Rural motorized groundwater is organized as mini-networks (ex-Scanwater stations, solar rehabilitations) serving standpipes -> outside the JMP borehole category. Rural borehole-category users therefore mostly PMH: 70-95% (lower bound reflects some rural/small-town private motorized boreholes in the wealthier south).
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized mini-networks: grid where available, else diesel/solar; standpipe users, not borehole users.
findings.caveats: Inventory partial (189/316 communes).

findings.source: Douala 5th municipality household survey (Water supply, sanitation and health risks in Douala 5, 2015: 42.3% of households on forages vs 33.8% CDE network; PAMJ 2018: two-thirds of Douala 5 households drinking borehole water); Douala drilling-market documentation
findings.quote: Douala 5: '42.30% of households used water from drilled wells (forages), 33.80% from [CDE] distribution network'. Douala's shallow sandy aquifer makes electric submersible boreholes cheap; the drilling market pitches 'pompes manuelles' for rural areas and electric immersed pumps for the city. Yaounde 2002: only 0.36% of households on boreholes (deep drilling costly). Urban borehole users are Douala-dominated and predominantly private motorized -> handpump share 10-30%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized boreholes: grid-electric (ENEO), generator backup among sellers; Douala grid better than Sahel but outage-prone.
findings.caveats: The 42.3%/two-thirds figures show borehole PREVALENCE, not the pump split - the split itself is inferred from technology/market evidence, so treat the 10-30 band as low-med confidence.

findings.source: CWSA via Ghana News Agency (Dec 2022): cumulative facilities provided to rural communities and small towns; CWSA Water Atlas (20,365 handpumps mapped in 6/10 regions, 2014, via Foster et al. 2019)
findings.quote: CWSA: '29,785 boreholes fitted with handpumps' vs '1,215 limited mechanised boreholes' plus 546 small-town piped systems. Handpump share of rural borehole POINTS = 29,785/(29,785+1,215) = 96%. Limited-mechanized points and small-town systems serve more users each (and small-town system users report standpipes/taps, exiting the borehole category), so the borehole-category USER share is set a bit lower: 75-95%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural mechanized: grid-electric where ECG/NEDCo reach, solar increasingly; small-town systems mostly grid/solar.
findings.caveats: CWSA counts are cumulative installations, not current functioning stock (26% non-functionality in 2014 atlas); private rural mechanized self-supply not in CWSA counts.

findings.source: Inference from Ghana self-supply literature (mechanized boreholes with poly-tanks widespread in peri-urban Accra/Kumasi/Ashanti) + persistence of handpumps in small towns classified urban in the 2021 PHC
findings.quote: No national urban pump-type user table. Urban Ghana's borehole-category users split between (a) private/compound mechanized boreholes with electric pumps and storage tanks - the dominant mode in metro fringes (Nigeria-like pattern, milder) - and (b) communal handpumps in the many small towns (5k-30k pop) counted as urban. Bounds 15-40%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban mechanized boreholes overwhelmingly grid-electric (Ghana's grid access ~85%+), generator backup less systematic than Nigeria.
findings.caveats: Ghana 2021 PHC lumps 'bore-hole/pump/tube well'; sachet water dominates urban drinking, so urban borehole users (~1-1.5M) are fewer than the rural.

findings.source: STUDI International 2015 national sample (2,214 handpumps) via Foster et al. 2019 Table 1; USAID/FHI360 DRC WSS sector profile; UNICEF DRC manual drilling program
findings.quote: 'An estimated 90 percent of the rural population depends on springs for drinking water' (USAID/FHI360 profile) - the rural borehole category is small. The boreholes that exist are donor/UNICEF program points fitted with handpumps (India Mark II / Afridev; manual drilling initiative); rural motorized boreholes essentially only occur inside small piped schemes (standpipe users). Handpump share of rural borehole users: 80-100%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Rural motorized rare; where present, solar mini-grids on piped schemes.
findings.caveats: MICS 2018 lumps the category; rural borehole users are a small minority of DRC's 4.4M borehole users' rural share given spring dominance.

findings.source: Inference: Kinshasa REGIDESO piped dominance with private motorized boreholes among wealthier households/water resellers, vs UNICEF-supported manually drilled handpump boreholes in peri-urban Kinshasa and secondary cities
findings.quote: Piped access fell from ~72% (MICS 2010) to <52% (MICS 2018), pushing urban households to alternatives: private electric boreholes (wealthy compounds, resellers - grid-electric with generator backup given SNEL outages) and manual-drilled handpump boreholes promoted by UNICEF in peri-urban zones. No user-share table found; bounds 15-50%.
findings.motorized_split_notes: Urban motorized: SNEL grid-electric, generator backup very common due to chronic outages.
findings.caveats: Weakest split in the set; Kinshasa dominates the urban borehole population.

research.region: West & Central Africa + Sahel (Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Chad, South Sudan, Guinea, Mali, Cameroon, Ghana, DR Congo)
research.summary: The region splits into two archetypes. In the francophone Sahel and South Sudan (BFA, TCD, MLI, GIN, SSD), rural water supply is institutionally standardized on forages equipped with pompes a motricite humaine (PMH): Burkina's INO 2015 counted 48,340 PMH-equipped forages out of 48,808 total forages (99%), with 6.34M people served at ~148 persons/PMH, and Guinea, Mali, Chad and South Sudan show the same structure in national inventories; critically, rural motorized groundwater in these countries is delivered through small piped schemes (AEPS/SHVA/mini-AEP/water yards) whose users fetch at standpipes and therefore report as JMP 'tap' users, not 'borehole' users — so the residual JMP tubewell/borehole category is 85-100% handpump. Even urban Chad is handpump-dominated: a 2017 N'Djamena survey found 79% of peripheral-district households using private (44%) or shared (35%) handpumps. The opposite archetype is the coastal/electrified metro (urban Nigeria, Douala, Accra fringe, Kinshasa) where borehole users run on private electric boreholes with storage tanks. Nigeria — the region's stakes-dominant case with ~81M borehole users — is quantified by the WASH-NORM 2021 national water-point census: urban borehole points are 14.8% handpump (6.6% vs 38.1% motorized, and only 33.5% of urban handpumps functional vs 68.5% of motorized), giving an urban handpump USER share of ~8-25%; rural borehole points are 39.3% handpump, and with communal handpumps serving far more users per point than private self-supply motorized boreholes, the rural user share is ~35-60%. Nigeria's motorized boreholes are 70.3% grid / 23.1% generator / 6.6% solar in urban areas and 48.2% / 36.5% / 14.4% in rural areas, with generator backup of grid-wired private boreholes ubiquitous — so the grid-only-failure scenario displaces materially fewer urban Nigerians than HEMP does. Ghana's CWSA inventory (29,785 handpump boreholes vs 1,215 limited-mechanized) puts rural Ghana at 75-95% handpump, while its metro fringe is mechanized. DR Congo is spring-dominated in rural areas (boreholes rare, handpump where present) with Kinshasa's borehole users mostly on motorized private supply. RWSN's Stop the Rot (2022) corroborates the pattern: ~200M people (18.5% of SSA; 25.9% rural, 7.3% urban) rely on ~700,000 handpumps, with the top-5 reliance countries (42-61% of population) including Burkina Faso, Guinea and South Sudan from this assignment.

regional_default.rationale: Rural default 70-95%: every national inventory examined (BFA INO, Mali DNH/SNV, Guinea SNAPE, Chad SDEA, Ghana CWSA, Cameroon PNDP, South Sudan IOM) shows community handpumps as the standard rural borehole technology, while rural motorized groundwater is organized as small piped/standpipe schemes whose users leave the JMP borehole category — the main exception is Nigeria (rural ~35-60%) where private self-supply motorized boreholes penetrated deep into rural areas, which is why Nigeria must be parameterized separately and not defaulted. Urban default 15-55% spans a real bimodality: coastal/electrified metros (Lagos-type, Douala, Accra, Kinshasa) sit at 8-30% handpump because private electric boreholes dominate, while Sahelian capitals with shallow aquifers, cheap manual drilling and weak grids (N'Djamena at ~75-95%, peri-urban Ouagadougou/Bamako) sit at 60-95%. For an uncovered country, pick the end of the urban range matching its archetype: grid reliability and aquifer depth are the best predictors — weak grid + shallow aquifer implies handpumps even in cities.

verifications.primary_source_checked: WASH-NORM 2021 (FMWR/NBS/UNICEF) full report PDF, independently retrieved via Wayback Machine snapshot of the cited UNICEF URL (web.archive.org/web/20260413012352/https://www.unicef.org/nigeria/media/5951/file/2021%20WASHNORM%20Report%20.pdf); checked Tables WF.B1 (p.260), WF.B2 (p.261), WF.B7-8 (p.266), HH.H1 (p.~300), and the functionality-by-type infographic on Executive Summary p.37 (rendered page image)
verifications.evidence_quote: Table WF.B1, Sector rows: Urban — hand pump borehole 6.3, force-lift hand pump borehole 0.3, motorized borehole 37.2, reticulated motorized 0.9, Total 100.0, N=917,937; Rural — 15.9, 0.9, 25.8, 0.2, N=1,395,629 (national total 2,313,566). Table WF.B2: Urban — solar 6.6, windmill 0.0, generator 23.1, public power supply 70.3 (N=349,709 motorised boreholes); Rural — 14.4, 0.9, 36.5, 48.2 (N=362,269). Exec summary p.37 'Functionality of All Facilities by Type': Handpump Boreholes 78%, Motorized Boreholes 64%, Improved Hand Dug Wells 67%, Public Stand Post 33%, Rainwater 69%. Summary text: '68.5% of privately owned were reported as functional, while the functionality of publicly owned water points is estimated at 52.8%.'
verifications.denominator_check: Correctly handled. The claimed shares are handpump/(handpump+motorized) among BOREHOLE water points only — urban 6.6/(6.6+38.1)=14.8%, rural 16.8/(16.8+26.0)=39.3% — reproduced exactly from Table WF.B1; improved hand-dug wells (urban 48.7%, rural 37.9% of points) are correctly excluded from both numerator and denominator, and the researcher correctly flags that these are point shares needing users-per-point conversion, and that household table HH.H1 (urban 35.1% of members on lumped 'tube well/borehole') cannot verify the split.
verifications.notes: Two strata verified in one record. RURAL 35-60: fully plausible, keep as claimed (point share 39.3% confirmed; functioning-point share recomputes to 44.1% with the report's real functionality figures; users-per-point reasoning pushes user share up). URBAN 8-25: point shares and WF.B2 power splits reproduce exactly, but one load-bearing sub-claim is REFUTED: the quoted functionality figures (urban handpump 33.5% functional vs motorized 68.5%; rural 62.9% vs 60.8%) appear NOWHERE in the report. WF.B7-8 gives functionality by sector only (urban 86.9%, rural 82.3%); the only by-type functionality data is national (exec summary p.37): handpump boreholes 78% functional — the HIGHEST of any type — vs motorized 64%. The 68.5% the researcher cited is national PRIVATELY-OWNED functionality; 33.5% matches nothing about handpumps (33% is public stand posts). The correction runs OPPOSITE to the researcher's: functioning-point handpump share is urban (6.6*0.78)/(6.6*0.78+38.1*0.64)=17.4%, not 7.8%, and rural 44.1%. This destroys the justification for the urban lower bound of 8; corrected urban bounds 10-25 with central ~15-17 (low end still allows reticulated/utility motorized points serving many users each; high end from communal-handpump users-per-point). Motorized power-split notes confirmed verbatim and safe to use for the non-HEMP scenario. Also note the report is internally inconsistent on overall functionality (62% narrative vs 77% infographic vs 84.1% in WF.B7-8), so treat any functionality adjustment as +/-10pp soft.
